findings.title: Count does not filter out inactive projects, so customers may be overbilled
findings.explanation: The neighbouring function is `activeProjectNames`, which presumably filters on a status such as archived, deleted or inactive. This query is `WHERE org_id = $1` only, so it counts every project row, including archived and soft-deleted ones. The result feeds invoicing, so any mismatch with the 'active' definition directly overcharges customers. Reuse the same predicate as `activeProjectNames`, ideally through a shared constant or helper so the two cannot drift. If archived projects really are billable, say so explicitly in the comment and in the PR description.

findings.title: Point-in-time count does not match a billing period
findings.explanation: The function counts the projects that exist at the moment it is called. An invoice covers a period, so projects created or deleted mid-period, or an invoice generated late or re-run, will give different totals. Decide the billing semantics (snapshot at period end, peak, or time-weighted). Then either take a period or `asOf` parameter or document that the caller must snapshot the value. Re-running the generator should give a reproducible result.

findings.title: No tests for billing-critical logic
findings.explanation: No tests are included. Add tests covering: an org with no projects (returns 0), archived or deleted projects being excluded, and projects belonging to other orgs not being counted. A pricing function needs this coverage before it goes live next month.

findings.title: Authorization relies on the caller and the comment is vague
findings.explanation: The function trusts `orgId` and does no access check, which is consistent with the sibling function. Make sure it is only called from the internal invoice generator and never with a user-supplied id. The comment 'one billable unit per project' should state exactly which projects count as billable. Also confirm that `projects(org_id)` is indexed, because the count scans every project in the org.
